points: The rescuer's own safety comes first, because a hurt rescuer cannot help the casualty.
Shout for help and alert the emergency services.
Keep the casualty in sight at all times.
Choose the safest method that will work, using the order of rescue methods.

notes.h: Order of rescue methods, safest first
points: 1. Talk: shout instructions to the casualty.
2. Reach: extend an arm, a pole or a towel from the bank.
3. Throw: throw a buoyant aid or a rope.
4. Wade: enter only if it is safe to do so.
5. Row: use a boat.
6. Swim: reach the casualty with an aid.
7. Tow: a contact tow, used only if the rescuer is trained and the tow is necessary.
Weak swimmer: a casualty who swims, but poorly.
Non-swimmer: a casualty who may panic and grab the rescuer.
Injured swimmer: a casualty who has been hurt in the water.
Unconscious casualty: a casualty who has lost consciousness and cannot help with the rescue.
Slide-in entry: used for unknown depth or conditions, and the safest entry; the rescuer enters feet first and slowly.
Step-in entry: used in known depth and clear water, and keeps the rescuer's eyes on the casualty.
Straddle entry: used in known deep water, with the head kept above the water so the rescuer can watch the casualty.
Compact jump: a jump from a height into known deep water.
Unknown conditions: always enter feet first, slowly, while testing the depth.
Head-up front crawl or head-up breaststroke keeps the casualty in sight during the approach.
Pace the approach to conserve energy for the return.
The lifesaving kick is an inverted breaststroke kick performed on the back.
Sidestroke is also used for towing.
Both are used when towing, because the arms are occupied with the casualty or the aid.
Stop at a safe distance of about 2 to 3 metres from the casualty.
Talk to reassure the casualty while stopped.
Offer an aid, such as a rescue tube or towel.
If the casualty grabs the rescuer, submerge to break free.
From the front, turn the casualty onto their back.
Turn smoothly, keeping the casualty's face clear of the water.
The casualty's face is out of the water once they are on their back.
The rescuer and the casualty both hold the aid, which keeps the rescuer out of reach of a panicking casualty.
Rigid aid: a rescue tube or float.
Non-rigid aid: a towel or clothing.
Chin tow: the rescuer supports the casualty by the chin.
Cross-chest or arm tow: the rescuer holds the casualty across the chest or arm.
Keep the casualty's face clear of the water throughout the tow.
Contact tows are used for tired or unconscious casualties.
Swim at a steady pace.
Breathe regularly.
Rest on an aid when tired.
Minimise movement in cold water.
Help the casualty out of the water with support.
Check the casualty's breathing.
Place the casualty in the recovery position, lying on their side to keep the airway clear.
Keep the casualty warm.
Seek medical help: a casualty rescued from water may still be at risk of secondary drowning.

notes.b: A weak swimmer is in difficulty near the edge.
points: 1. Lie flat on the bank.
2. Reach with a pole, or throw a buoyant aid.
3. Talk the casualty in towards the edge.

notes.h: Worked rescue: swimming rescue with an aid
points: 1. Enter with a slide-in entry, feet first and slowly, testing the depth.
2. Approach head-up, so the casualty stays in sight.
3. Stop about 2 to 3 metres from the casualty, talk to reassure them and offer the aid.
4. Tow the casualty with a non-contact tow, both holding the aid, using the lifesaving kick.
5. Land the casualty, helping them out with support.

keyTerms.definition: A slow, feet-first entry into water of unknown depth or conditions, the safest type of entry.
An entry into known depth and clear water in which the rescuer steps in and keeps their eyes on the casualty.
An entry into known deep water in which the rescuer's head stays above the water.
A jump from a height into known deep water.
A tow in which the rescuer and casualty both hold a rigid or non-rigid aid, keeping the rescuer out of reach.
A tow in which the rescuer holds the casualty directly, by the chin or across the chest or arm.
An inverted breaststroke kick performed on the back, used when towing because the arms are occupied.
A position with the casualty lying on their side to keep the airway clear.
A casualty who cannot swim and may panic and grab the rescuer.

factCards.term: Order of rescue methods, safest first
factCards.definition: Talk, reach, throw, wade (only if safe), row, swim with an aid, then tow (contact tow, only if trained and necessary).

factCards.term: Which entry keeps the head above water in known deep water?
How far should a rescuer stop from a panicking casualty?
factCards.definition: About 2 to 3 metres, then talk to reassure the casualty and offer an aid.

factCards.term: What does a non-contact tow use as its aid?
factCards.definition: A rigid aid such as a rescue tube or float, or a non-rigid aid such as a towel or clothing.

factCards.term: Aftercare after landing a casualty, in order
factCards.definition: Help out with support, check breathing, recovery position, keep warm, seek medical help.

questions.prompt: Describe the order of rescue methods a lifesaver should consider, and explain why the order matters.
questions.model: The order, safest first, is talk, reach, throw, wade (only if safe), row, swim with an aid, and tow. Talk and reach keep the rescuer out of the water altogether. Throwing a buoyant aid also keeps the rescuer on land while giving the casualty support. Wading, rowing and swimming with an aid each add risk to the rescuer, so they are used only when the earlier methods will not work and it is safe. A contact tow comes last because the rescuer is then in the water with a casualty who may panic and grab them. The order matters because the rescuer always chooses the method that gives the casualty the most help for the least risk to themselves.

questions.prompt: Describe a suitable entry into water of unknown depth and explain why it is used.
questions.model: The slide-in entry. The rescuer enters feet first and slowly, sliding into the water while testing the depth with the feet, so that they do not dive into shallow water or unseen obstacles. It is the safest entry because the rescuer finds the depth and any hazard before the head goes under, which avoids a head or neck injury from diving or jumping into unknown water.
